subsection: 10. Society during World War II: the Home Front, rationing, evacuees, refugees, collaboration and resistance

notes.h: Total war and the civilian: why the Home Front mattered
notes.b: In the Second World War the fighting was not confined to soldiers on distant fronts. Whole populations and economies were put to work for the war, and civilians became targets, so what ordinary people did and endured is part of the history of the war itself.
points: Total war means a war in which a state mobilises its whole population and economy, and in which civilians become targets. This is why the Home Front was decisive in 1939-1945: factories, farms, food supplies and morale could win or lose the war as surely as battles did.

For civilians the war ran in stages. Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939. The Phoney War followed (months with little fighting), then the fall of France (armistice 22 June 1940).
The Battle of Britain and the Blitz came next, and by 1942 most of Europe was occupied. The Allied bombing offensive and liberation in 1944-45 came last.
Before 1939 governments expected air attack on cities to cause huge casualties and panic. This fear is why Britain planned evacuation, shelters and the blackout in advance.
Nazi racial ideology ranked peoples, so occupation in the east was far harsher than in the west. This shaped rationing, forced labour and resistance, as the later blocks show.
notes.tip: Exam answers on civilians score for specific, dated experience, not a general narrative of the war. Learn the dates and cause-and-result pairs in the blocks that follow.

notes.h: Operation Pied Piper: the evacuation of British cities
notes.b: Britain's government expected German bombers to devastate the cities, so it planned to move the people it thought most at risk, above all children, out to the countryside before the war began. The first movement took place in the first days of September 1939.
points: Operation Pied Piper, the government's evacuation scheme from London, Birmingham, Liverpool, Manchester and other big cities, began on 1 September 1939. It moved schoolchildren with their teachers, mothers with young children, expectant mothers and the disabled, because these groups were judged most at risk and least able to protect themselves.

Evacuees travelled by train,  with luggage labels on their coats and gas masks in boxes. The government organised billeting (the placing of evacuees in private homes), and householders could be required to accept them.
About 1.5 million people were evacuated in the first few days, most of them children. This was a vast movement of people, planned in advance because of the expectation of air raids.
Operation Pied Piper, the evacuation of civilians in September 1939, is not Operation Dynamo, the Dunkirk evacuation of troops in May-June 1940.
notes.tip: Learn the three facts examiners reward for evacuation: it began on 1 September 1939, it moved about 1.5 million people, and most of them were children. Do not confuse Pied Piper with Dunkirk.

notes.h: Evacuees: reception, the drift back and later waves
notes.b: Evacuation did not go smoothly, because it threw together families from very different backgrounds. Its results ran from lasting friendships to a new awareness of how poor much of urban Britain was.
points: Reception was mixed. Some hosts and evacuees formed lasting bonds, while others met homesickness, culture clash and hostility. Evacuees were received unevenly in the countryside.
Some middle-class hosts were shocked by lice, poor clothing, poor hygiene and unfamiliar behaviour, and by the poor health of children from poor urban homes.
When the expected bombing did not come during the Phoney War, many evacuees drifted back to the cities, and most had gone home by early 1940.
There were further waves of evacuation in 1940, after the fall of France and when the Blitz began, and again in 1944 against the V-1 flying bombs.
Overseas evacuation was a separate scheme, run by the Children's Overseas Reception Board (CORB) in 1940, to send children to the Dominions and the USA.
The overseas scheme ended after the liner City of Benares was sunk by a U-boat in September 1940, because 77 of the 90 CORB children on board died.

Evacuation showed the comfortable classes the poverty of the inner cities. Reformers used its social findings to argue for better health and education services, so it strengthened the case for social reform after the war.
notes.tip: A common cause-and-result question asks why evacuation mattered. Give the reason (fear of bombing), the drift back in the Phoney War, and the result (awareness of poverty feeding reform).

notes.h: Why Britain rationed, and the order of rationing
notes.b: Britain imported much of its food, and German U-boats sank the merchant ships that carried it. Rationing, a fixed allowance for each person, shared scarce food fairly and helped keep prices down.
points: Each household registered with a shopkeeper and received ration books. Shoppers handed in coupons as well as money, so everyone had a fixed weekly allowance whatever their income.
Petrol was rationed from September 1939. Bacon, butter and sugar were rationed on 8 January 1940, and meat followed in March 1940, each with a fixed weekly allowance.
Tea and margarine were rationed in July 1940, and clothing on 1 June 1941, by coupons. A points system for tinned and dried goods began in December 1941, and sweets were rationed in 1942.
Rationing lasted beyond the war because shortages continued. Bread was rationed in 1946-48, though never during the war, and all rationing ended in 1954, with meat last in July 1954.
notes.tip: If asked for the start of rationing, give January 1940 and name bacon, butter and sugar. Also explain why it was needed: imports, U-boats and fair shares.

notes.h: The Ministry of Food, Utility goods and Dig for Victory
notes.b: The government did more than ration. It organised food supply, standardised everyday goods and asked people to grow their own, so that a nation short of imports could stay healthy.
points: The Ministry of Food, led by Lord Woolton from April 1940, controlled food imports, supply and prices. It also ran publicity and recipes, and basic foods included National Dried Milk and the wholemeal National Loaf (from 1942).
Children and mothers received extra milk and vitamins, such as orange juice and cod liver oil. British Restaurants were subsidised communal restaurants serving cheap meals.

Utility goods were standard designs of clothing (from 1941-42) and furniture (from 1943) sold at controlled prices, with minimum standards of design and quality. The Make Do and Mend campaign urged people to repair clothes rather than buy new.
The Dig for Victory campaign, from 1939, encouraged families to grow vegetables in gardens, allotments and parks, so that less food had to be imported and more land was ploughed.
The Women's Land Army, re-formed in 1939, recruited women, called Land Girls, to work on farms. This raised home food production.

Most people accepted rationing as fair. The diet of the poorest improved, and children's health held up or improved. There were still shortages, queues and a black market, run by dealers known as spivs.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level paragraphs reward accurate dated facts: January 1940 for bacon, butter and sugar, Woolton, the National Loaf, Dig for Victory and the Land Army. Pair each measure with its effect.

notes.h: The Blitz and shelter
notes.b: From September 1940 German bombers attacked British cities by night. The Blitz tested the country, and the shelters and the blackout were the everyday defences against it.
points: The blackout, enforced from 1 September 1939 by ARP (Air Raid Precautions) wardens, hid cities from bombers. It also raised road deaths sharply in the first winter, because streets and vehicles were unlit.

Anderson shelters were garden shelters, issued from 1939 and free to households below an income limit, while others paid. Morrison shelters were indoor shelters from 1941. Public shelters and London Underground stations were also used, and people took over the Underground despite official reluctance.

The Blitz began on 7 September 1940 with raids on London's docks and the East End. London was bombed on 57 consecutive nights, and raids continued until May 1941, the heaviest on London being 10-11 May 1941.

Other cities suffered too. Coventry was bombed on 14 November 1940, which destroyed the city centre and cathedral and killed about 550 to 600 people. Clydebank was hit in March 1941, and Belfast in April and May 1941, with about 900 killed in the raid of 15-16 April 1941.
Liverpool, Birmingham, Glasgow, Bristol, Plymouth and Hull were also heavily bombed.

The Blitz of September 1940 to May 1941 killed over 40,000 civilians, about half of them in London. About 60,000 civilians were killed by bombing in Britain in the whole war, though sources give 60,000-70,000.
Many homes were destroyed, which left people homeless and dependent on rest centres, places where bombed-out families were given shelter and help.
notes.tip: Examiners want dates, cities, shelters and casualties. Give 7 September 1940, 57 consecutive nights, and 'over 40,000, about half in London'. Do not mix the Blitz (autumn 1940 to May 1941) with the Phoney War.

notes.h: Civil defence, the Home Guard and morale
notes.b: Surviving the Blitz depended on thousands of volunteers and on keeping up spirits. The government used propaganda and the media, and later historians have questioned how united the people really were.
points: Civil defence was staffed by ARP wardens, the Auxiliary Fire Service, fire-watchers, and ambulance and rescue workers, many of them part-time volunteers. The Women's Voluntary Service (WVS), founded in 1938 and led by Lady Reading, provided welfare work, including meals and clothing for bombed-out families.

The Local Defence Volunteers were formed in May 1940 after Anthony Eden's broadcast appeal, so that ordinary men could help resist invasion, and renamed the Home Guard in July 1940. Mostly older men and those in reserved jobs, they guarded against invasion and supported civil defence.
The Home Guard stood down in 1944.

The Ministry of Information used posters and slogans such as Careless Talk Costs Lives, and censorship, to shape opinion. BBC news, Churchill's broadcasts, comedy such as ITMA (It's That Man Again, starring Tommy Handley) and cinema newsreels and films carried official messages.
Mass Observation, a social research organisation founded in 1937, was independent of the government. Its reports on morale and public opinion were used by the Ministry of Information.
From June 1944 V-1 flying bombs, and from September 1944 V-2 rockets, fell on London and the south-east, killing thousands of civilians. About 6,000 were killed by V-1s and about 2,700 by V-2s.

The 'Blitz spirit' is the idea of a united, cheerful people under the bombs, and it was contemporary propaganda. Historians such as Angus Calder (The People's War, 1969; The Myth of the Blitz, 1991) show fear, looting, class anger (especially at the East End's suffering) and complaints alongside real endurance.
In short, morale bent but did not break. The shared danger and rationing also encouraged support for government planning and the welfare reforms after 1945.
notes.tip: Do not claim that the Blitz broke morale or that it did not affect it. Say morale bent but did not break, with fear and anger recorded alongside endurance. Mass Observation was independent, not a government body.

notes.h: Work, women and conscription in Britain
notes.b: Fighting a total war meant directing labour. Men were conscripted, workers were steered into war industry, and women entered work and service on a new scale.
points: Ernest Bevin, a trade union leader, was Minister of Labour and National Service from May 1940 to 1945 in Churchill's coalition. He had power to direct workers into war industries, and reserved occupations kept key workers out of the forces.

Men were conscripted (called up by law) under the National Service (Armed Forces) Act of 3 September 1939. From December 1943 some conscripts, the Bevin Boys, were chosen by ballot to work in the coal mines.

Women's war work grew greatly, so women worked in factories making munitions and aircraft, and in transport, farms and offices. Women also served as nurses and in anti-aircraft batteries, but not in front-line combat.

The women's auxiliary services were the ATS (Auxiliary Territorial Service, the army), the WAAF (Women's Auxiliary Air Force) and the WRNS (Women's Royal Naval Service, 'Wrens'). The Women's Land Army was a civilian service for farms.

The National Service (No. 2) Act of December 1941 made unmarried women and childless widows aged 20 to 30 liable to conscription (call-up) into the auxiliary services, civil defence or industry. It was later extended, though married women with young children were exempt.

Change had limits. Women were usually paid less than men for the same work, and nurseries were limited. Most women expected, or were expected, to leave paid work after the war, but attitudes had begun to change.
Northern Ireland was part of the UK Home Front, with Belfast's Harland and Wolff shipyard, Short Brothers aircraft works and the 1941 Blitz, but conscription was not applied there.
notes.tip: Be exact about the 1941 Act: it made women aged 20 to 30 liable to call-up, not just registered. Keep Bevin (Minister of Labour) apart from Bevan (NHS) and Beveridge (the report).

notes.h: The Beveridge Report and the road to the welfare state
notes.b: The war made ordinary people want a better country afterwards. Beveridge's report gave that wish a plan, and the governments of 1944-48 turned the plan into law.
points: Sir William Beveridge's report, Social Insurance and Allied Services, was published on 1 December 1942. It named five giants to be defeated: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness.

It proposed a single national insurance scheme, in return for weekly contributions, often summed up as 'from the cradle to the grave'. It also proposed family allowances, a national health service and the aim of full employment.
The report sold hundreds of thousands of copies, which shows huge public interest. Churchill's coalition was cautious, while Labour was enthusiastic.
The report was a plan, not law, and it did not itself create the welfare state. The coalition's Education Act 1944 (R.A. Butler) came first, then the Family Allowances Act 1945.

Labour won the general election of July 1945, and Clement Attlee became Prime Minister. The National Insurance Act 1946 followed, and the National Health Service began on 5 July 1948 under Aneurin Bevan, Minister of Health.
The war had made state planning and 'fair shares' acceptable, which helps explain why the reforms had such wide support.
notes.tip: The long-term result of the Home Front is the welfare state, but do not say Beveridge wrote the NHS Act. Name the five giants and credit the Acts of 1944-48 for carrying the plan out.

notes.h: Germany's Home Front: rationing, women and total war
notes.b: Germany's civilians faced the same demands of war as Britain's, but the Nazi regime handled them differently. It took food and labour from occupied Europe and was cautious about asking Germans to sacrifice, until defeat at Stalingrad.
points: Rationing began at the end of August 1939, just before the war. Rations were relatively adequate until the later war years because Germany took food from occupied Europe, but they were cut in 1942 and there was severe shortage in 1944-45.
Ration scales were graded by work and by race, so that German civilians received higher rations than foreign workers and occupied populations, and Jews and eastern workers received far less.

Nazi ideology kept women's call-up limited in 1939-42, and the regime preferred foreign labour. Many German women already worked in 1939, so the number in paid work rose little in the war. Historians such as Richard Overy stress this; the older claim that German women hardly worked is wrong.
After Stalingrad, where the German Sixth Army surrendered in early February 1943, Goebbels made his total war speech at the Berlin Sportpalast on 18 February 1943.

The regime then, because manpower was running out, registered women for labour service and closed non-essential businesses. Albert Speer, Minister of Armaments from 1942, drove up armaments output, and the Volkssturm (a home militia of men aged 16 to 60) was formed in October 1944.
Women's employment rose less than in Britain, so Britain mobilised its own people, women included, more fully.

Control and terror kept order at home. The SD (the SS security service) reported on public mood, 'defeatism' was punished harshly and listening to foreign radio was a crime, and terror rose as defeat neared. The July 1944 plot was part of the opposition.
notes.tip: For Germany, show the shift from limited mobilisation to total war after Stalingrad, and say that German women already worked in 1939. Examiners reward a Britain-Germany contrast.

notes.h: Germany's Home Front: foreign labour, bombing and evacuation
notes.b: Because the regime held back its own women and drafted its men, Germany filled factories and farms with foreign workers. From 1942 its cities were also bombed, and civilians suffered both ways.
points: By 1944 about seven to eight million foreign civilian workers and prisoners of war, from all over occupied Europe, were in the German economy. Fritz Sauckel was in charge of labour recruitment from 1942.

Western workers were treated better than eastern ones, because Nazi racial ideology ranked eastern peoples lower. Ostarbeiter ('eastern workers') from the USSR, and Poles, wore badges (Ostarbeiter an 'OST' badge), lived in camps and suffered hunger, beatings and high death rates from disease, overwork and mistreatment.
Firms also used concentration-camp prisoners as labour.

RAF area bombing of cities began in 1942 under Arthur Harris, head of Bomber Command, and was joined by American daylight raids. The Hamburg firestorm of late July 1943, killed about 40,000 (estimates 35,000 to 45,000).

Dresden was bombed on 13-15 February 1945, killing up to about 25,000. German civilian deaths from bombing in the whole war are estimated at about 350,000 to about 600,000, with great loss of housing and many left homeless.
Morale was damaged but the regime did not collapse, and production rose until 1944. The effect on production is debated.

The Kinderlandverschickung (KLV), run with the Hitler Youth from 1940, evacuated millions of children and families from bombed cities to the countryside. It is not the Kindertransport or British evacuation.
notes.tip: In broad essays, credit the dependence on forced foreign labour and its brutality, and the bombing of cities. Do not say that bombing 'failed' or 'won the war': it killed and destroyed hugely but did not break the regime.

notes.h: Refugees and displaced people
notes.b: War and occupation uprooted millions of people. Whether they were fleeing, interned, exiled or freed, their fate depended on the policies of the governments they met.
points: Before the war, about 10,000 mainly Jewish children reached Britain on the Kindertransport in 1938-39, fleeing Nazi persecution.

In May and June 1940, millions of Belgians, Dutch and French fled the German advance, the French 'exodus'. They crowded and blocked the roads of northern and central France and were strafed from the air.

After the fall of France, Britain interned about 27,000 German, Austrian and Italian 'enemy aliens' in 1940, many of them Jewish refugees from Nazism. Most were held on the Isle of Man, and some were shipped overseas to Canada and Australia. Most were released by 1941.
The Arandora Star, carrying German and Italian internees to Canada, was sunk by a U-boat on 2 July 1940, and over 800 died.

London hosted governments in exile: Poland (from 1940), Norway, the Netherlands, Belgium and Czechoslovakia. De Gaulle's Free French were in London from June 1940, and exiles served in the Allied forces.
In the east, Germans were settled in annexed Polish lands and Poles were expelled, and in 1941 the Soviet Union moved people and industry eastward.
In 1945 millions of displaced persons (DPs) were found: former forced labourers, prisoners of war and camp survivors.

UNRRA (the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, set up in November 1943) and the Allied armies ran DP camps and repatriation, though many eastern Europeans and Jewish survivors would not or could not go home.
More than ten million Germans fled or were expelled from eastern Europe in 1944-47.
notes.tip: Marks go to named movements with dates, not 'many people fled'. Use the 1940 exodus, internment and the Arandora Star, governments in exile in London, DPs and UNRRA in 1945, and the expulsions of Germans.

notes.h: Collaboration: meaning and motives
notes.b: Most occupied countries were run, at least in part, with the help of some of their own people. To judge collaboration fairly we need to know the forms it took and the reasons people gave.
points: Collaboration means cooperation with the occupier. It ranged from state collaboration by governments and officials, through economic collaboration by firms and workers, to collaborationism, which is ideological support for Nazism, including joining German units.

Collaboration forced by circumstance must be kept apart from willing collaboration, because a worker obeying orders is not the same as a volunteer for the SS. Attentisme (waiting to see what happens) is neither collaboration nor resistance.
People collaborated out of belief in Nazism or fascism, anti-communism, ambition and profit, a wish to protect their country or job, fear, and the belief in 1940 that Germany had won.
Waffen-SS units recruited volunteers in western Europe, including Norwegians, Dutch, Belgians and French. Auxiliaries also served in the east.
notes.tip: Collaboration questions reward definitions with examples from more than one country and the motives. Also state the judgement that most people neither collaborated nor resisted.

notes.h: Collaboration country by country
notes.b: The occupied states show collaboration in different forms, from a puppet government in Norway to a 'model protectorate' in Denmark. In each case it carried consequences for Jews and for the country after liberation.
points: Norway: Vidkun Quisling led the fascist party Nasjonal Samling (founded 1933). He proclaimed himself head of government on 9 April 1940, the day of the German invasion, but the Germans soon set him aside.
Quisling was Minister-President from 1 February 1942 under the real ruler, Reichskommissar Josef Terboven, with little popular support. His name became a word for traitor.

The Netherlands: the civil service and police kept working under Reichskommissar Arthur Seyss-Inquart. Anton Mussert's NSB (National Socialist Movement) cooperated, and Dutch police helped round up Jews. About three-quarters of the Jews of the Netherlands were killed.

Belgium: King Leopold III surrendered the Belgian army on 28 May 1940 and stayed in Belgium. Léon Degrelle's Rexists (Rex) and Flemish nationalists collaborated, and Degrelle fought on the Eastern Front in the Waffen-SS.

Denmark was occupied on 9 April 1940 and was a 'model protectorate'. The Danish government and parliament carried on until the government resigned in August 1943. This collaboration by negotiation spared Danes the worst until then.
Vichy France was the largest case of state collaboration. Pétain met Hitler at Montoire in October 1940, and Laval headed the Vichy government from April 1942.

Vichy helped in the deportation of Jews (the Vel' d'Hiv round-up in Paris, July 1942) and supplied labour to Germany. The Milice, formed in January 1943, carried out reprisals against resisters. There is more on this in the notes on France and Vichy.
After liberation there were trials and executions, purges and summary revenge. Laval and Quisling were executed in October 1945, and Mussert in 1946.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Quisling (Norway), Mussert (Netherlands), Degrelle (Belgium) and Pétain and Laval (France). Learn one example from each country with its date.

notes.h: Resistance: forms and outside help
notes.b: Resistance was not only armed. Most of it was small acts of defiance, and it depended on help from outside that kept it supplied and connected.
points: Resistance ranged from passive and symbolic acts, such as go-slows, jokes and refusing to cooperate, to underground newspapers, intelligence, escape lines for airmen, hiding Jews, strikes, sabotage and armed partisan war.

Britain's Special Operations Executive (SOE, set up in July 1940) and later American agents supplied arms, radios and agents, because resisters could not make these themselves. The BBC carried messages to resisters, and the resistance supplied intelligence in return.
The French Resistance and the Polish Home Army were both linked to Allied intelligence and special operations, which provided weapons, radio equipment and training.
The cost was high. Reprisals and hostage shootings, the destruction of villages, and the torture and execution of captured resisters followed.

notes.h: Resistance in France, Poland, Yugoslavia and Germany
notes.b: The strength, politics and risks of resistance depended on the country and on the occupier. These four cases are the ones examiners most often name.
points: France: the Free French (de Gaulle's forces abroad) and the internal Resistance, including the maquis (rural armed groups, swollen by evaders of the STO, the compulsory labour service of February 1943), carried out sabotage before D-Day. Jean Moulin united the movements and died in 1943.
Reprisals followed, for example at Oradour-sur-Glane on 10 June 1944, where the SS killed more than 600 villagers. There is more on this in the notes on France and Vichy.

Poland: the Home Army (Armia Krajowa, AK), formed in February 1942, was usually described as the largest underground army in occupied Europe. It was loyal to the Polish government in exile in London, and part of a Polish Underground State with underground schools and courts.

The Warsaw Uprising ran from 1 August to 2 October 1944. About 150,000 to 200,000 civilians were killed. The Red Army stood on the far bank of the Vistula and did not help, and the Germans then largely destroyed the city.

Yugoslavia: Josip Broz Tito's Communist partisans fought the Germans, Italians and the Croatian Ustaša (the fascist regime under Ante Pavelić) from 1941, after Germany invaded in April 1941. They also fought a civil war, because of rivalry, against Draža Mihailović's royalist Chetniks.
Britain switched its support to Tito in 1943. The partisans liberated most of the country, with the Red Army helping take Belgrade in October 1944, and Tito then ran a post-war Communist state.

Germany: the White Rose was a group of Munich University students who distributed six leaflets against the regime in 1942-43. Hans and Sophie Scholl were arrested on 18 February 1943 and executed on 22 February 1943.

Other German opposition included Communist groups, youth gangs such as the Edelweiss Pirates (working-class youths, some executed in Cologne in 1944), the churches, and the July 1944 plot (20 July 1944). Resistance was hard in a police state among one's own people.
notes.tip: Keep the Warsaw Uprising (Home Army, 1944) apart from the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising (1943), which belongs elsewhere. Do not confuse Tito's Communist partisans with Mihailović's royalist Chetniks.

notes.h: Other notable acts of resistance, and its significance
notes.b: Some of the best-known acts of resistance came from small countries and happened in a single moment. Taken together they show both what resistance achieved and why historians weigh its limits.
points: Norway: Norwegian commandos trained by SOE sabotaged the Vemork heavy-water plant in February 1943, and teachers refused to join a Nazi union.
The Netherlands: the February Strike in Amsterdam on 25-26 February 1941 was a protest against the round-up of Jews, for example a rare mass act of public defiance.

Czechoslovakia: Czech and Slovak parachutists trained in Britain attacked Reinhard Heydrich in Prague on 27 May 1942, and he died in June. In reprisal, the village of Lidice was destroyed in June 1942, with men shot and women and children deported.

Denmark: after a warning of a planned round-up in early October 1943, ordinary Danes ferried about 7,000 Jews, most of the community, across the Øresund to neutral Sweden. The story that the Danish king wore the yellow star is a legend.

Soviet partisans fought behind German lines. Italian partisans fought the Germans and Mussolini's Salò Republic from September 1943, and partisans shot Mussolini in April 1945. The Italian resistance became a major political force after liberation.

Resistance had military value in intelligence, sabotage and tying down German troops, especially in Yugoslavia and the USSR. It also had political value: national self-respect, post-war governments formed by resistance movements, and prestige for the Communists.
Its limits were small numbers until 1943-44 and heavy losses from reprisals.
notes.tip: Resistance questions reward named examples: the Danish rescue, Yugoslav liberation, the Home Army and the White Rose. Balance achievements (intelligence, sabotage, post-war legitimacy) against limits (a minority, heavy reprisals, Warsaw's destruction).

notes.h: Civilians in occupied France
notes.b: For French civilians, occupation meant shortage, fear of reprisal and divided loyalties. Comparing this with the British experience is a standard essay.
points: France was divided into two zones, and the Germans occupied the southern zone as well on 11 November 1942. German soldiers requisitioned buildings and food, and curfews, identity checks and the taking of hostages made daily life uneasy.

Ration cards were issued by age and work category, and bread, meat, fat and fuel were short. There were queues and substitutes, prices rose and city dwellers went hungry, so many made trips to the countryside to buy food on the black market.
About 1.8 million French soldiers were taken prisoner in 1940, and well over a million were still in Germany years later.
Women had to take over family farms, shops and families because so many men were away. The STO (February 1943) sent young men to work in Germany or into the maquis.
Jews were persecuted and deported, which Vichy helped carry out. There is more on this in the notes on France and Vichy.
Allied bombing of French industry and railways before and after D-Day, and the battles of 1944, killed tens of thousands of French civilians.

Attitudes changed over time. Most people accepted Pétain in 1940, but the compulsory labour service and the German occupation of the south in November 1942 turned many against Vichy and the Germans from 1942-43.
Attentisme ('wait and see') was the commonest response, and only minorities actively resisted or collaborated.
French women were given the vote by de Gaulle's provisional government in 1944 and first voted in 1945.
notes.tip: For the France half of an essay, give the zones, shortage and black market, prisoners of war, the STO, persecution of Jews, reprisals and attentisme. Use 'well over a million prisoners of war'.

notes.h: Comparing Britain with France and with Germany
notes.b: Examiners expect a judgement, not a list. The three societies shared rationing and bombing but not their fate, because Britain was never occupied.
points: Britain was bombed but never occupied, so it kept democracy and a free (if censored) press, and the war united society and led to reform.
France was defeated, occupied and divided by collaboration and resistance, so it emerged from the war with bitter memories.

Britain and Germany both rationed, evacuated and were bombed. Britain mobilised its own people, women included, more fully, while Germany relied on forced foreign labour and the exploitation of occupied Europe.
notes.tip: Top marks need a comparative judgement: bombed but free and united, against defeated, occupied and divided, and short-term against long-term effects.

notes.h: Assessment: civilians in the Second World War
notes.b: Judgements of wartime society balance the solidarity and sacrifice of civilians against fear, division and the wide scale of collaboration. The balance has changed as historians have looked beyond wartime propaganda.
points: Achievement: British society sustained the war effort through rationing, evacuation and civil defence, and the Beveridge Report reshaped post-war social policy. Morale held and production rose.
Limit: the British Home Front had class tensions and a black market, and women were paid less than men, so change for women was limited. The 'Blitz spirit' was partly a myth.
Limit: Germany's home front relied on forced foreign labour, so its civilians were protected by the systematic exploitation of occupied peoples.
Achievement: resistance movements kept political opposition alive, so they gave national self-respect and provided the bases for post-war governments in France, Italy and Yugoslavia.
Limit: most people in occupied Europe neither resisted nor collaborated actively. Resistance remained a small minority until 1943-44, and it brought heavy reprisals.
Contemporary view: the British public generally accepted the sacrifices of the war and supported the welfare plans that followed. In Britain, the 'people's war' was a widely shared picture.

Later view: Angus Calder challenged the Blitz spirit, and Robert Paxton (Vichy France, 1972) revised the post-war myth of a nation in resistance in France. Historians have since found widespread accommodation elsewhere too, and research since the 1970s shows a more complex and divided record.
In short, resistance and collaboration were two ends of a range in which most people lay in between.
notes.tip: Pair each achievement with a limit and each contemporary view with a later one. Use the moral record of resistance against the scale of collaboration and attentisme.

keyTerms.definition: Cooperation with an occupying power, including the supply of labour, police help and political support for the occupation.
Organised opposition to an occupying power or a regime, including sabotage, intelligence gathering, propaganda and armed action.
The civilian population of a country at war and the work, rationing, evacuation and bombing that shaped its daily life.
The official allocation of limited supplies of food, fuel and clothing to each person or household during wartime.
The movement of children and vulnerable civilians from cities to safer areas, as organised in Britain under Operation Pied Piper in 1939.
A person who has fled from their home country or region because of war, persecution or occupation.
A term for a collaborator with an occupying power, taken from Vidkun Quisling, who headed a collaborationist government in Norway from 1942.
The government evacuation of schoolchildren and others from British cities that began on 1 September 1939.
The 1942 report that proposed a national insurance system and named five giants of want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness.
The enforced darkening of lights at night to hinder enemy bombers.
Forced labourers from the Soviet Union and eastern Europe who worked in Germany, treated more harshly than western workers.
Rural bands of French resisters, swollen by young men avoiding forced labour in Germany in 1943 and 1944.

Lord Woolton led the Ministry of Food from 1940, controlling food supply and prices.
The Blitz began on 7 September 1940 and London was bombed on 57 consecutive nights between September and November 1940.
The Local Defence Volunteers were formed in May 1940 and later renamed the Home Guard.
Published in December 1942, the report named want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness as the five giants to be defeated.
The December 1941 Act required single women aged 20 to 30 to register for war work.
Vidkun Quisling headed a collaborationist government in Norway from February 1942.

factCards.term: Polish Home Army: formation and uprising
factCards.definition: The Armia Krajowa was formed in 1942 and fought in the Warsaw Uprising of August to October 1944.
Hans and Sophie Scholl were executed in Munich in February 1943 for distributing leaflets against the Nazi regime.

factCards.term: Danish Jews: rescue date and destination
factCards.definition: In October 1943 most Danish Jews were ferried to Sweden, with more than 7,000 escaping.
Josip Broz Tito led the Yugoslav partisans, who fought German, Italian and Croatian forces from 1941.
A ship carrying internees to Canada, sunk by a U-boat with the loss of over 800 lives.
The German scheme to send children from bombed cities to the countryside.
Young men sent from December 1943 to work in the coal mines instead of military service.
The Home Army rose in Warsaw in August 1944 and was crushed by early October.
The National Insurance Act of 1946 and the NHS of 1948 carried out most of its proposals.
